result.markdown: # Data visualization {#sec-visualization} Julia has three reasonable routes to graphics, all resting on [**Makie.jl**](https://docs.makie.org) [@danisch2021makie]: | Route | For whom | |---|---| | `TidierPlots.jl` | people coming from `ggplot2` who want the same grammar | | `AlgebraOfGraphics.jl` | people who want an idiomatically Julian grammar of graphics | | Plain `Makie.jl` | full control over the figure | This chapter shows all three on the same data, because the right choice depends on the task — and because knowing how to translate between them keeps you from getting stuck. ::: {#cell-setup-06 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using TidierData using CairoMakie using AlgebraOfGraphics using CSV, DataFrames CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png") ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("..", "data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) ponds_c = @chain ponds begin @drop_missing(canopy) @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2)) end nrow(ponds_c) ``` ::: {#setup-06 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 173 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Exercises in this chapter A figure cannot be checked automatically, so in most *Your turn* boxes you compare your plot with the one in the solution. Start each session by loading the packages and the data, with the book folder open in VS Code: ```julia include("exercises/check.jl") using TidierData, TidierPlots, CairoMakie, AlgebraOfGraphics, CSV, DataFrames, Statistics ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) ponds_c = @chain ponds begin @drop_missing(canopy) @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2)) end ``` ::: ## `TidierPlots.jl`: the ggplot grammar {#sec-tidierplots} ::: {#cell-fig-tidierplots-scatter .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using TidierPlots ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = canopy, y = richness, color = region)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "Canopy cover (%)", y = "Species richness", title = "Richness declines with shading") ``` ::: {#fig-tidierplots-scatter .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Richness against canopy cover, by region. ::: ::: ::: {.r-equivalent} **In R** ```r ggplot(ponds_c, aes(x = canopy, y = richness, colour = region)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "Canopy cover (%)", y = "Species richness") ``` The translation is nearly character for character; the difference is the `@` in `@aes`. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.1 — Richness and temperature Redo @fig-tidierplots-scatter with water temperature (`temp_c`) on the x axis and the points coloured by hydroperiod (`hydro`). Label both axes. Does richness change with temperature as clearly as with canopy? There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Only the `@aes` mapping and the labels change. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-6-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = temp_c, y = richness, color = hydro)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "Water temperature (°C)", y = "Species richness") ``` ::: {#answer-6-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The cloud is much flatter than for canopy. The simulation does include a temperature effect (`scripts/make_data.jl`), but a small one: about 3% more species per degree, invisible next to the scatter between ponds. ::: ::: ## `AlgebraOfGraphics.jl`: an algebraic grammar {#sec-aog} AoG treats plots as an algebra: `*` combines layers, `+` superimposes them. ::: {#cell-fig-aog-scatter .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) * mapping(:canopy => "Canopy cover (%)", :richness => "Species richness", color = :region => "Region") * (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear()) draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 450),)) ``` ::: {#fig-aog-scatter .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` The same plot in AlgebraOfGraphics, with a linear fit per region. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} `AlgebraOfGraphics.data` and `AlgebraOfGraphics.linear` are qualified because the names `data` and `linear` collide with other loaded packages. In a script using only AoG, `data(...)` and `linear()` suffice. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.2 — Body size, with fitted lines With AlgebraOfGraphics, plot `body_size` against `temp_c`, coloured by `hydro`, with a linear fit for each hydroperiod. Do permanent and temporary ponds differ? There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Start from the block above and change the `mapping`. The fitted lines follow the colour grouping automatically. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-6-2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) * mapping(:temp_c => "Water temperature (°C)", :body_size => "Body size (mm)", color = :hydro => "Hydroperiod") * (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear()) draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 450),)) ``` ::: {#answer-6-2 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The two lines almost coincide: in the simulation, body size depends on temperature and canopy but not on hydroperiod. We test this formally in @sec-linear-models. ::: ::: ## Facets {#sec-facets} ::: {#cell-fig-facets .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) * mapping(:log_area => "log(area)", :richness => "Richness", color = :region, layout = :hydro) * (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear()) draw(plt; figure = (size = (800, 400),)) ``` ::: {#fig-facets .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Richness–area relationship faceted by hydroperiod. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.3 — Facets in the ggplot grammar Translate @fig-facets to `TidierPlots.jl`, using `facet_wrap` to split the panels by hydroperiod. Leave out the fitted lines (see the warning in the solution). There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint `facet_wrap(facets = :hydro)` is added with `+`, like any other layer. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-6-3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = log_area, y = richness, color = region)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + facet_wrap(facets = :hydro) + labs(x = "log(area)", y = "Richness") ``` ::: {#answer-6-3 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## A limit of TidierPlots In `TidierPlots.jl` 1.0.0 (checked in September 2026), adding `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` to a faceted plot fails with `column name :facet not found`. `geom_smooth` works without facets, and facets work without `geom_smooth`, but not together. When the ggplot grammar reaches a limit like this, AlgebraOfGraphics (@fig-facets) is the way out. ::: ::: ::: ## Distributions {#sec-distributions} ::: {#cell-fig-boxplot .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) * mapping(:region => "Region", :richness => "Richness", color = :hydro => "Hydroperiod", dodge = :hydro) * visual(BoxPlot) draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 420),)) ``` ::: {#fig-boxplot .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Richness distribution by region and hydroperiod. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.4 — The shape of a distribution Boxplots hide the shape of a distribution. Show the distribution of `body_size` in each region as violins (`Violin`), with one colour per region. There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Replace `BoxPlot` with `Violin` and map `region` to both the x axis and `color`. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-6-4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) * mapping(:region => "Region", :body_size => "Body size (mm)", color = :region) * visual(Violin) draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 420),)) ``` ::: {#answer-6-4 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Plain `Makie.jl`: full control {#sec-makie} When a figure needs a layout the grammar cannot express, drop down to Makie. ::: {#cell-fig-makie-composite .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (860, 380)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Canopy cover (%)", ylabel = "Richness", title = "(a) Canopy") scatter!(ax1, ponds_c.canopy, ponds_c.richness, color = (:steelblue, 0.6)) ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "log(area)", ylabel = "Richness", title = "(b) Area") scatter!(ax2, ponds_c.log_area, ponds_c.richness, color = (:darkorange, 0.6)) ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "Richness", ylabel = "Frequency", title = "(c) Distribution") hist!(ax3, ponds_c.richness, bins = 12, color = (:seagreen, 0.7)) fig ``` ::: {#fig-makie-composite .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A composite figure assembled by hand with Makie. ::: ::: Makie's layout system is grid-based (`fig[row, col]`), covering the role of `patchwork` and `cowplot` in R without an extra package. ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.5 — Two panels by hand Build a figure with `size = (800, 350)` and two panels: on the left, a boxplot of richness by region; on the right, a bar chart of the proportion of ponds with the focal species in each region (the numbers from 5.4). Store it in `fig_regions`. There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Makie's `boxplot!` and `barplot!` want numbers on the x axis. Give each region a number with `[findfirst(==(r), regs) for r in ponds.region]`, where `regs = ["Amazon", "Atlantic", "Cerrado"]`, and put the names back with `xticks = (1:3, regs)` in each `Axis`. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-6-5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} regs = ["Amazon", "Atlantic", "Cerrado"] idx = [findfirst(==(r), regs) for r in ponds.region] props = [mean(ponds.focal[ponds.region .== r]) for r in regs] fig_regions = Figure(size = (800, 350)) ax1 = Axis(fig_regions[1, 1], xticks = (1:3, regs), xlabel = "Region", ylabel = "Richness", title = "(a) Richness") boxplot!(ax1, idx, ponds.richness, color = (:steelblue, 0.6)) ax2 = Axis(fig_regions[1, 2], xticks = (1:3, regs), xlabel = "Region", ylabel = "Proportion of ponds", title = "(b) Focal species") barplot!(ax2, 1:3, props, color = (:darkorange, 0.8)) fig_regions ``` ::: {#answer-6-5 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The two panels tell different stories: richness differs sharply between regions, focal-species occurrence hardly at all. ::: ::: ## Saving figures {#sec-saving} ::: {#saving .cell execution_count=0} ``` {.julia .cell-code} save("figure.png", fig; px_per_unit = 3) # high-resolution raster save("figure.pdf", fig) # vector, for publication save("figure.svg", fig) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 6.6 — A figure for publication Save `fig_regions` from 6.5 as `focal-by-region.png`, at three pixels per unit, in the book folder. Then check the file: `check("6.6", "focal-by-region.png")`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The block above shows the keyword that sets the resolution. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#answer-6-6 .cell execution_count=0} ``` {.julia .cell-code} save("focal-by-region.png", fig_regions; px_per_unit = 3) check("6.6", "focal-by-region.png") ``` ::: An 800 × 350 figure at three pixels per unit gives a 2400 × 1050 px image — enough for a two-column journal figure. For vector output, save as `.pdf` instead. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Choosing a backend `CairoMakie` produces publication-quality static output (PNG, PDF, SVG) and is what this book uses. `GLMakie` opens GPU-accelerated interactive windows — useful for exploring data, unsuitable for rendering a book. ::: ## Challenges {.unnumbered} 1. In 6.1 you judged the temperature effect by eye. Add a linear fit per hydroperiod with `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`. Does the line change your reading of the plot? What would you need to know before trusting it? 2. Panel (b) of 6.5 shows proportions without uncertainty. Add an error bar of $\pm 2$ standard errors to each bar, with $\text{SE} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ and `errorbars!`. Do the regions still look different? 3. Redo @fig-makie-composite with one colour per region in every panel and a single shared legend on the right (`Legend(fig[1, 4], ...)`).
